target: AG1’s claim that making Election Day a national holiday would remove scheduling barriers and increase accessibility
objection: A national holiday by itself does not guarantee paid time off for the private-sector workers who most need it; federal holiday status mainly affects government jobs, while retail, food service, and other hourly workers may still have to work and can even lose pay, so low-income workers may remain constrained.

target: AG1’s implication that a holiday is the best way to increase turnout
objection: More reliable approaches already exist, such as laws requiring employers to give time to vote with pay protections and reforms like automatic or opt-out voter registration; research also suggests a holiday alone is less effective at boosting turnout than these targeted access reforms.

target: AG2’s claim that a national holiday alone does not help because it does not force private employers to provide paid leave
objection: The main barrier is schedule conflict, not just employer pay policy. A national holiday would still reduce conflicts by making schools and many workplaces less likely to operate normally, and it can be paired with enforceable time-to-vote or paid-voting protections for private employees.

target: AG1’s argument that a holiday would reduce schedule conflict by changing the day’s normal operations
objection: That underestimates low-income hourly workers, who are often in retail, food service, caregiving, and similar jobs that keep running even on holidays. Without guaranteed paid time off, a holiday can still leave them working, unpaid, or using scarce PTO to vote.

target: AG1’s suggestion that holiday status is an effective lever if combined with other protections
objection: If the proposal needs enforceable paid time-off or voting-window protections to work, then the holiday itself is redundant; the direct worker-protection laws are the real mechanism, and holiday status may pass while those protections are weakened or only partly applied.

target: AG2’s framing that holiday status and time-to-vote/pay protections are either-or choices
objection: The two policies solve different parts of the same problem: employer rules do not address school, childcare, and caregiving schedules, while a national holiday changes those baseline household schedules and lowers the transaction costs of voting by making the day off the default.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday reduces household and transaction costs enough to matter
objection: That still does not solve the main problem for low-income workers. Household schedules may not align with services like childcare and transportation, and if private employers stay open, employees still face wage loss or voting-time loss; without enforceable private-employer rules, a holiday does not reliably lower costs for those most constrained.

target: AG2’s objection that a holiday is insufficient because private employers may remain open
objection: Even a partial calendar shift matters: school, childcare, and caregiving routines change when Election Day is a holiday, and workers are less dependent on asking permission or trading off pay. Holiday status reduces reliance on employer discretion and can complement, not replace, paid voting protections.

target: AG1’s assertion that a holiday would broadly reduce friction and can be packaged with worker protections
objection: A national holiday is still a weak and inequitable lever because the benefits may not reach the workers facing the biggest constraints: low-income hourly employees may still need to work or lose pay, while higher-income workers already have more flexibility. If paired protections are what matter, the holiday is mostly redundant and can add political risk or legislative dilution.

target: AG2’s claim that holiday status is not enough because it does not force every private employer to pay or close
objection: Defaults change behavior: time-to-vote rules require people to know their rights, request time, coordinate with managers, and risk denial, whereas a national holiday makes voting the default allowed activity and reduces the uncertainty and friction that deter turnout, even if it does not fully replace time-off laws.

A holiday does not meaningfully change what private employees can actually do because federal holiday status does not guarantee paid time off in the private sector. If employers stay open, hourly workers still face the same work-versus-vote or unpaid-time tradeoff, so the policy does not reliably remove the main barrier.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday cannot change private-sector realities
objection: A national Election Day holiday changes the labor-market environment by creating expectations that schools and many institutions will close, customer traffic will drop, and staffing will adjust. That makes employers more likely to grant paid time or reduce hours, so the holiday shifts default routines even if it does not directly rewrite pay rules.

target: AG1’s argument that holiday status will alter the labor-market environment and make employers more accommodating
objection: Holiday status does not ensure pay continuity for private workers. Employers may keep shifts running or cut hours and pay around the holiday, leaving low-income hourly workers with the same core choice between working and missing voting time or losing wages/PTO, which can even widen unequal burdens.

target: AG2’s focus on private-employer pay continuity as the central issue
objection: A national Election Day holiday can also reduce the overall time cost of voting by improving election administration: more people are available during the day, polling place staffing and voter flow may be easier, and wait times can be shorter, so the holiday helps with both work conflicts and the practical burden of voting itself.
